title: Tenses: Form, Use and Consistency
summary: All 12 English tenses with their forms, uses and signal words, the common mistakes to avoid, how to keep your tense consistent, and the tense questions Checkpoint asks, with practice and answers.

blocks.text: 1. What a tense is and why it matters

A **tense** is the form of a verb that shows **time** (past, present or future) and **aspect** (whether the action is simple, in progress, or completed). English has **12 tenses**: three times (past, present, future) × four aspects (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous).

You will not be asked to name tenses in Checkpoint 8, but tenses matter in two ways. In **reading**, you may be asked why a writer chose a tense (for example, the present tense in a story, or the past perfect for a flashback). In **writing**, accurate verb forms and a consistent tense are part of the grammar mark, and examiners notice tense errors quickly.

blocks.title: Key words
items: **V1** = base form (go, write, take). **V2** = past simple (went, wrote, took). **V3** = past participle (gone, written, taken).
**Auxiliary (helping) verb**: be, have, do, will used to build tenses, questions and negatives.

**Simple** = the whole action as a fact. **Continuous** = the action in progress (be + V-ing). **Perfect** = completed before a point in time (have + V3). **Perfect continuous** = duration up to a point (have been + V-ing).
**Signal words**: time words that usually go with a tense (yesterday, since, by the time, at the moment).

blocks.text: 2. The 12 tenses at a glance

rows: Habits, facts, timetables. Also used for immediacy in some stories and for reviews
The ferry leaves at six. Water boils at 100°C.
Happening now · temporary situations · fixed future plans
We are crossing the bridge now.
Past action with a present result · experience · recent news
The council has closed the park.
Action that started in the past and is still going (focus on duration)
They have been waiting for two hours.
Finished actions at a known past time · the main tense of stories
She opened the letter and gasped.
An action in progress in the past. Background to a story event
It was raining when the bus broke down.
An action before another past action (flashback)
By the time we arrived, the show had started.
Duration up to a point in the past
He had been running for an hour when he fell.
An action in progress at a future time
This time next week, we will be flying to Aswan.
By June, I will have finished the book.
Duration up to a future time
In May, she will have been teaching for ten years.

blocks.text: 3. Present tenses: form and signal words

rows: always, usually, often, sometimes, never, every day, on Fridays
now, right now, at the moment, currently, Look! Listen! this week
just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, so far, recently
for, since, all day, lately, how long

items: Present simple with he / she / it adds **-s / -es**: he watches, she goes, it flies. Questions and negatives use **does / doesn't + V1** (no -s on the main verb): Does it fly? not Does it flies?
Use **since** + a point in time (since 2020, since Monday) and **for** + a period of time (for three years, for a week).

**Present perfect or past simple?** If you say when it happened (yesterday, in 2022, last week), use the past simple: I visited Luxor last year. If the time is not stated or is still continuing, use the present perfect: I have visited Luxor twice.

blocks.text: 4. Past tenses: form and signal words

rows: yesterday, ago, last night, in 2019, when I was young
while, when, as, at 8 p.m. yesterday, all evening
before, after, by the time, already, when (the earlier action)
for, since + a past point, before, when

items: **Past simple vs past continuous**: the long background action is in the past continuous, the short action that interrupts it is in the past simple: While I **was cooking**, the phone **rang**.

**Past simple vs past perfect**: when two past actions are told out of order, the **earlier** one takes the past perfect: When we reached the platform, the train **had left**. (it left first). Compare: When we reached the platform, the train left. (it left as we arrived).
After **did / didn't**, always use **V1**: Did she see it? She didn't see it. (not Did she saw, didn't saw).

blocks.text: 5. Future forms: form and signal words

rows: tomorrow, next week, soon, I think, probably, I promise
I'**m not going to give up**.
plans already decided, or evidence now (Look at those clouds!)
I **will be sitting** my exam at nine.
this time tomorrow, at 10 o'clock next Monday
by + time, by the time, before, by then
By June, I **will have been learning** French for a year.
How long **will** you **have been living** here?
by... for, by the time... for

blocks.text: **Present continuous for the future**: for fixed arrangements with a time and place, English often uses the present continuous: We **are meeting** the head teacher at ten tomorrow.

blocks.title: State verbs are not used in continuous tenses
items: Verbs that describe a **state**, not an action, are usually not used with -ing: know, believe, understand, want, need, like, love, hate, prefer, own, belong, seem, mean, remember.
I am knowing the answer. ✗ → I **know** the answer. ✓
This bag is belonging to Salma. ✗ → This bag **belongs** to Salma. ✓

blocks.text: 6. Irregular verbs you must get right
Many tense errors in exam writing are wrong past forms. Learn the V2 and V3 of these common irregular verbs.
7. Keeping your tense consistent

Choose one **main tense** for a piece of writing and stay in it. Stories are usually told in the **past simple**, with the past continuous for background and the past perfect for anything that happened earlier. Reports, reviews and information texts are usually in the **present simple**.

blocks.title: The tense mistake examiners see most
blocks.text: Switching tense by accident in a story: She ran to the door and opens it. Choose one main tense (usually the past simple) and stay in it, unless you deliberately move to a flashback (past perfect).

rows: The wind howled and the windows shake.
The wind howled and the windows shook.
Karim picks up the box and realised it was empty.
Karim picked up the box and realised it was empty.
Every morning we wake at six, and then we had breakfast.
Every morning we wake at six, and then we have breakfast.

blocks.text: **When a change of tense is correct:**

items: A **flashback** (past perfect): She stared at the photo. Ten years earlier, she **had lived** in that house.
**Dialogue** keeps the speaker's own tense: "I **am** scared," she whispered.
**General truths** stay in the present: He learnt that the Nile **flows** north.
A **deliberate shift** to the present to create immediacy at the climax of a story (use it once, on purpose, not by accident).

blocks.text: 8. Common mistakes

rows: A finished time (yesterday) needs the past simple.
since + a situation still true now needs the present perfect.
I was went to the shop.
Do not add was to a past simple verb.
When I arrived, everyone left. (meaning they had already gone)
When I arrived, everyone had left.
The earlier action takes the past perfect.
After has / have / had, use V3.

blocks.text: 9. How Checkpoint asks about tenses
**In reading** you may be asked why a writer uses a particular tense, or what a change of tense shows. Learn these effects:

items: **Present tense in a story** makes the action feel immediate, as if it is happening now, which increases tension: I open the door. Something moves.
**Past perfect** signals a **flashback**: the story steps back to an earlier time (Years before, he had lived here).
**Present tense in non-fiction** (travel writing, reviews, information texts) makes the facts sound current and true.
**Future tense** in persuasive writing makes promises and predictions sound certain: This plan will save lives.
**Past continuous** sets the scene and shows background action: Rain was falling and the street lamps were flickering.
**A change of tense** often marks a change of time in the text (a memory, or a return to the present).

blocks.text: **Exam-style example.** The market is waking up. Traders unload crates of mangoes, a boy balances a tray of bread on his head, and the smell of fresh coffee drifts between the stalls.

**Question:** Why does the writer use the present tense in this travel description? **Answer:** It makes the scene feel as if it is happening right now, in front of the reader, so the description is more vivid and the reader feels present in the market.

**In your writing**, show control and range: use the past simple for the main events, the past continuous for background, the past perfect for earlier events, and keep the tense consistent. In non-fiction, use the present tense for facts and the future tense or will for predictions and promises.

blocks.title: الأزمنة في الكتابة

بعد did و didn't الفعل يرجع للمصدر: didn't go مش didn't went.
لو قلت امتى حصل الحدث (yesterday, last week) استخدم الماضي البسيط، مش have.

blocks.text: 10. Practice

items.q: Correct the tense error: Hana walked to the window and sees a light in the garden.
items.a: Hana walked to the window and saw a light in the garden. (keep the past tense)

items.q: Why might a writer suddenly change from the past tense to the present tense in a story (I ran. I hid. Now I am waiting in the dark.)?
items.a: To make the moment feel immediate, as if it is happening right now, which increases tension and draws the reader into the scene.
have lived (present perfect with since, the situation is still true).

items.q: Complete: While we ______ (eat) dinner, the lights went out.
items.a: were eating (past continuous for the longer background action interrupted by a short one).

items.q: Complete: By the time we reached the station, the train ______ (leave).
items.a: had left (past perfect: the train left before we arrived).

items.q: Complete: This time tomorrow, I ______ (sit) my science exam.
items.a: will be sitting (future continuous: in progress at a future time).

items.q: Correct: I have visited Aswan last summer.
items.a: I visited Aswan last summer. (last summer is a finished time, so use the past simple).

items.q: Correct: Did your brother finished his project?
items.a: Did your brother finish his project? (after did, use V1).

items.q: Omar stared at the empty desk. Years earlier, his grandfather had written his first poem there. Name the tense of had written and explain why the writer uses it.
items.a: Past perfect. It signals a flashback: the writer steps back to an earlier time to give background about the grandfather, before returning to the main story.

items.q: Rewrite in one consistent past tense: The storm arrives at midnight. Trees fell across the road and the power goes off.
items.a: The storm arrived at midnight. Trees fell across the road and the power went off.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: One main tense per text. did / didn't + V1. has / have / had + V3. Finished time = past simple. Earlier past = past perfect.
